title: I have overcome the world (John 16:16–33)
hook: sorrow turns to joy like a woman after labor

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Advocate, the one called to your side. Your line was into all truth. Did you take one step on that decision? Day six hundred thirty-eight.

"A little while." Jesus says it, and the disciples start whispering to each other across the table. What does he mean, a little while? A little while and you won't see me, and again a little while and you will. They want to ask him, but nobody does. It's late, he's been talking about leaving all evening, and every new sentence seems to make things more confusing. But he notices them whispering. He knows what they want to ask. And instead of a definition, he gives them a picture. One that anyone who has been in a delivery room will recognize.
screen: `A LITTLE WHILE? WHAT DOES HE MEAN?`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "A woman when she is in travail hath sorrow, because her hour is come: but as soon as she is delivered of the child, she remembereth no more the anguish, for joy that a man is born into the world." Travail is labor. And notice what the picture does. The pain isn't swapped out for something else. The same event that hurts is the event that brings the joy. The sorrow turns into joy, the way labor turns into a baby in your arms. The prophets used this image too, for Israel waiting on God's new day. Jesus applies it to the next few days. They will weep while others rejoice. Then they'll see him again, "and your joy no man taketh from you." Then the chapter's last line, the one in today's carry: "In the world ye shall have tribulation: but be of good cheer; I have overcome the world." Two honest halves. You will have trouble: no promise that life gets easy. And then, be of good cheer. The Greek is tharseite: take courage, be brave, cheer up. It's the same word he says elsewhere in the Gospels to frightened people. And the reason: I have overcome. The Greek verb is nikao, to win, to conquer. You may know the related word nike, victory. And it's in a tense that speaks of something already done. He says it the night before the cross, before anything looks like winning. Christians hear in that the heart of their hope: the victory is spoken before it is seen.
screen: `THE SAME EVENT THAT HURTS BRINGS JOY.`
`NIKAO: SPOKEN BEFORE IT LOOKS LIKE WINNING.`
then, large: `BE OF GOOD CHEER; I HAVE OVERCOME THE WORLD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: take heart in one trouble. Settle, and breathe. Name one trouble you're in right now. Not the whole list. One. Say it plainly to yourself, the way Jesus says it: in the world you will have this. Don't pretend it's smaller than it is. Then breathe in, and on the out-breath, let yourself hear the second half: take courage. Do it a few times. If you pray, you can bring that trouble to God with his words: be of good cheer. If you don't, simply let courage sit beside the trouble. The bell holds the time.
I have overcome the world. Said the night before the cross: trouble is real, and the victory is spoken before anyone can see it.
screen: `I HAVE OVERCOME THE WORLD — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: be of good cheer. Today, when the trouble you named shows up, say both halves to yourself: this is real, and take courage. Day six hundred thirty-eight.

howItsDone: Christians often turn to John 16:33 in hard seasons, as a word of courage spoken before the worst had happened.

fork.setup: your friends are whispering, confused about 'a little while'. it's late. what do you do?
options: give them a picture: a woman in labor, then joy.
say they'll understand when they're older.
fork.reveal: he answers with the picture of childbirth: sorrow that turns into joy, and joy no one can take.

original.note: Greek: I have overcome, I have conquered. from nikao; in the perfect tense, something done whose result stands.

trapdoor: what you thought: be of good cheer means cheer up.
what it means: two honest halves. you will have trouble, and take courage, because he has overcome.
what a scholar hears: tharseite, the Gospels' word for 'take courage', and nenikeka, a perfect tense, said before the cross as if the victory were already won.

notes: Childbirth imagery in the prophets (Isaiah 26:17–19; 66:7–14). Confirm the general statement.
tharseite used elsewhere in the Gospels to frightened people (e.g., Matthew 14:27; Mark 6:50). Confirm.
nenikeka (perfect tense) in John 16:33. Confirm form and pronunciation.
The hook paraphrases John 16:16–19 (the disciples asking among themselves).
